references.text: Jesus had already determined to go to Jerusalem. [ref:Luk 9:51|Luke 9:51] states that "when the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem." This shows Jesus' firm resolve to complete his journey toward Jerusalem, which aligns with "it is necessary (δεῖ) that I walk" in Luke 13:33.

Jesus predicts his suffering and death in Jerusalem. In [ref:Luk 9:22|Luke 9:22] he says that the Son of Man "must (δεῖ) suffer many things and be rejected" – the same divine "must" (δεῖ) as in 13:33, expressing God's plan and necessity.

Again Jesus predicts his suffering in Jerusalem. In [ref:Luk 18:31-33|Luke 18:31-33] he says that "everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled" – he will be handed over, mocked, mistreated, and killed in Jerusalem.

Even as a twelve-year-old, Jesus uses the expression "δεῖ" (it is necessary) regarding his mission. In [ref:Luk 2:49|Luke 2:49] he says: "Did you not know that I must (δεῖ) be in my Father's house?" This shows that divine necessity governs all of Jesus' life and work.

The risen Jesus explains that "everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to (δεῖ) be fulfilled" ([ref:Luk 24:44|Luke 24:44]). The divine necessity in 13:33 points forward to the fulfillment of God's plan of salvation.

Jerusalem was known as the place where prophets were persecuted and killed. In [ref:2 Kong 21:13|2 Kings 21:13] Jerusalem's judgment is mentioned, within the context of King Manasseh's reign when innocent blood was shed, including the tradition that the prophet Isaiah was killed in Jerusalem.

The prophet Zechariah was stoned in the temple courtyard in Jerusalem, as described in [ref:2 Krøn 24:21|2 Chronicles 24:21]. This is a concrete example of a prophet being killed in Jerusalem, which Jesus refers to with the statement that "a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem".

In [ref:2 Krøn 36:15-16|2 Chronicles 36:15-16] it is described how the people of Jerusalem mocked God's messengers, despised his words, and ridiculed the prophets. This pattern of persecuting prophets in Jerusalem underlies Jesus' words in Luke 13:33.

Nehemiah confesses that the people "were stubborn; they rebelled against you and cast your law behind their backs. They killed your prophets" ([ref:Neh 9:26|Nehemiah 9:26]). This confession confirms the historical pattern Jesus points to – that prophets were killed.

In [ref:Jer 26:20-23|Jeremiah 26:20-23] it is told about the prophet Uriah, who prophesied against Jerusalem and was brought back and killed by King Jehoiakim. This is yet another example of prophets being killed in connection with Jerusalem.

Jesus utters similar words in [ref:Matt 23:37|Matthew 23:37]: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you." This parallel passage confirms that Jerusalem had a reputation for killing prophets, which is the point of Luke 13:33.

The following verse [ref:Luk 13:34|Luke 13:34] expands on the same thought: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you." Jesus laments over Jerusalem's pattern of rejecting and killing God's prophets.

Stephen accuses Jerusalem's leaders in [ref:Apg 7:52|Acts 7:52]: "Which of the prophets did your ancestors not persecute? They killed those who announced beforehand that the Righteous One would come." This confirms the tradition Jesus refers to in Luke 13:33.
